text: Earlier in this path, defense in depth meant layering controls around one system -- a perimeter, hardened hosts, application validation, logging, all wrapped around one application. At true enterprise scale, the thing being defended usually isn't one system. It's a federation: multiple business units, subsidiaries, and acquired companies, each with its own legacy technology and its own risk tolerance.

So the layering has to span that whole federation. One central identity provider with single sign-on and conditional access, as the spine every business unit plugs into. Network segmentation not just within a data center, but between business units, subsidiaries, and operational technology versus corporate IT. A shared data classification scheme and DLP baseline. One EDR baseline across the fleet, including companies you've acquired that are still running whatever antivirus they had before the deal closed. And a central SOC with visibility across all of it -- a SOC that only sees one business unit is blind to an attacker who pivots from one unit into another.

The 2013 Target breach is worth revisiting here, because it's a segmentation failure, not a missing-patch story. Attackers got in using a third-party HVAC vendor's credentials, through a vendor-management segment of the network, and moved from there into the systems handling point-of-sale and cardholder data. The individual controls existed. The segmentation between a vendor-facing function and the payment environment didn't actually isolate them from each other.
That's the pattern to design against at enterprise scale: a breach rarely stays confined to the business unit it started in, because the segmentation between business functions wasn't real.

You can't realistically force every business unit onto identical controls on identical timelines -- legacy systems, budgets, and regulatory obligations differ too much. What works is a centralized minimum baseline every unit must meet, combined with a real, tracked exception process: a documented, time-bound waiver with a named owner and a remediation plan for units that can't meet it yet. That keeps the baseline honest instead of becoming a document nobody follows -- the organization-wide version of the tradeoff thinking from Lesson 2.
Next, we connect all of this to the business itself: why the same technical risk needs a genuinely different architectural response at a startup than it does at a regulated bank.
